papers.title: EWSR1::ATF1 hyperactivation via TRIM11 depletion triggers lethal metabolic rewiring in clear cell sarcoma
papers.abstract: Clear cell sarcoma (CCS) is an ultra-rare and aggressive soft tissue sarcoma driven by the EWSR1::ATF1 fusion oncoprotein. Currently, no effective and well-tolerated treatment options are available to CCS patients. Direct inhibition of fusion transcription factors is precluded by the absence of defined ligand-binding pockets, whereas their abundance is under the control of the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS), offering an alternative avenue for biology-guided treatment. Here we show the abundance of EWSR1::ATF1 is tightly regulated by the UPS, and that release of this constraint is lethal to CCS cells. A reporter-based CRISPR/Cas9 knockout screen of UPS components identified TRIM11 as an E3 ligase that regulates turnover of EWSR1::ATF1, which it recognises as a neosubstrate without altering wild-type EWSR1 or ATF1. Depletion of TRIM11 increased nuclear fusion protein abundance, amplified the fusion-driven transcriptional programs and reduced viability. Proteomic analysis identified the cataplerotic enzyme phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase 1 (PCK1), a direct EWSR1::ATF1 target, as the key mediator of lethal effects of fusion hyperactivation. Extracellular flux analysis, isotope tracing and quantitative metabolomics revealed excessive cataplerotic carbon withdrawal and impaired oxidative phosphorylation as the underlying mechanism. In patient tumors, high PCK1 expression associated with metastatic transcriptome programs and disease presentation, as well as shorter survival. Taken together, we report that hyperactivation of EWSR1::ATF1 opens a metabolic vulnerability, establishing TRIM11 as an actionable dependency and PCK1 as a candidate prognostic biomarker in CCS.

papers.title: Protecting host mitochondria with vitamin B3 preserves bioenergetics and thermogenesis during antibiotic treatment
papers.abstract: Antibiotics that target bacterial translation can also impair mitochondrial function because mitochondria retain bacterial-like ribosomes. As antibiotic resistance continues to increase and the use of several broad-spectrum antibiotics has been limited by their mitochondrial toxicity, there is a growing need to understand their off-target effects in host physiology, and to identify strategies that can mitigate antibiotic-induced mitochondrial dysfunction. We demonstrate that antibiotic chloramphenicol (CA) induces a dose-dependent reduction in mitochondrial respiration and mitochondrial thermogenesis in Drosophila S2 cells, human HEK293T cells and in developing Drosophila larvae. In vivo, CA exposure triggers female-biased aberrant innate immune activation of hosts carrying naturally occurring mitochondrial rRNA variants. Metabolomic profiling revealed alterations in vitamin B3 metabolism in Drosophila during and following CA exposure. Among the vitamin B3 vitamers examined, nicotinamide (NAM) exhibited the strongest protective effect, mitigating the CA-induced impairments in mitochondrial respiration and thermogenesis, as well as aberrant immune activation. We identify mitochondrial thermogenesis as a previously unrecognized target of antibiotic-induced mitochondrial perturbation and a sensitive marker of mitochondrial stress. Furthermore, we demonstrate that co-supplementation of CA with NAM mitigates antibiotic-induced mitochondrial toxicity through evolutionarily conserved mitochondrial pathways. Finally, we establish Drosophila as a powerful model for investigating antibiotic-induced mitochondrial dysfunction and for developing therapeutic strategies to protect host mitochondria during antibiotic treatment.

papers.title: A global post-transcriptional regulator directs Acinetobacter baumannii carbon preference and gut colonization
papers.abstract: Acinetobacter baumannii is a multidrug-resistant pathogen that colonizes the gut, increasing the risk of subsequent infection and transmission. Recent work showed that A. baumannii catabolizes ornithine, a non-preferred carbon source, to colonize the gut. However, the mechanisms of carbon preference were unknown in A. baumannii. Here, experimental evolution identified the conserved RNA-binding protein CsrA as a regulator of carbon preference in A. baumannii, a previously unreported CsrA function. RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing (RIP-Seq) revealed hundreds of CsrA-associated transcripts. A. baumannii CsrA directly bound and repressed expression of the ast arginine/ornithine catabolic operons. The Pseudomonas aeruginosa CsrA homolog RsmA repressed arginine/ornithine catabolic operon expression, suggesting this CsrA function extends to other bacterial taxa. Finally, CsrA was required for competitive fitness during A. baumannii gut colonization. These findings uncover a previously unrecognized role for a global regulator in A. baumannii carbon preference and persistence in the gut, a critical reservoir for multidrug-resistant pathogens.

papers.title: Alveolar and airway progenitors converge on an epigenetically encoded profibrotic state
papers.abstract: During organ regeneration, epithelial transitional states arise from progenitors and instruct the mesenchyme to remodel the extracellular matrix. However, the identity of the progenitors, the mechanisms underlying this transition, and why these states persist in tissue fibrosis often remain elusive. Here, using lineage tracing in mice, we show that the profibrotic KRT5-/KRT17+ state in pulmonary fibrosis arises convergently from alveolar type (AT) 2 and airway secretory cells. AT1 cells generate neither KRT5-/KRT17+ nor AT2 cells. TGF-{beta}/SMAD3 acts through KMT2A and p300 to epigenetically reprogram human AT2 cells into the KRT5-/KRT17+ state. In human pulmonary fibrosis, KRT5-/KRT17+ cells slough off, and transitional cells re-epithelialize the denuded basement membrane. Transcriptionally convergent states arise in injured kidney, skin, and intestine. This work reframes fibrogenesis as the accumulation of a conserved profibrotic transitional state via ongoing turnover, not persistence alone, and nominates the state transition and its epigenetic regulators as therapeutic targets.

papers.title: Replication-stress response shapes Leishmania genome plasticity through non-equivalent RAD9 and HUS1 functions.
papers.abstract: Genome plasticity, manifested as gene copy-number variation and mosaic aneuploidy, enables adaptation in Leishmania , yet how genome-surveillance pathways shape this variation remains unclear. Here we show that partial depletion of HUS1 or RAD9, subunits of the conserved 9-1-1 checkpoint clamp, produces opposing replication-stress responses and contrasting patterns of genome remodelling in Leishmania major . During methotrexate selection HUS1 deficiency restricted DHFR-TS amplification and favoured linear amplicons, whereas RAD9 deficiency was associated with extensive circular amplification. This divergence extended to genome-wide scale: HUS1-deficient cells carried fewer but larger candidate rearrangements, whereas RAD9-deficient cells retained a largely wild-type rearrangement burden. These differences were accompanied by distinct HUS1 and RAD9 occupancy profiles around repetitive DNA implicated in gene amplification. Deficiency of either of these factors also resulted in differing effects on aneuploidy. While HUS1-deficient cells showed limited shifts towards chromosome disomy, RAD9-deficient cells exhibited broader chromosome copy-number gains and losses. Together, these findings identify replication-stress surveillance as a determinant of parasite genome plasticity, revealing that perturbing individual subunits of the same checkpoint complex can produce opposing genome-remodelling outcomes and reshape the variation available for adaptation.

papers.title: Measuring the strength of selection and pollen limitation on flower colour along an urban rural cline in Hesperis matronalis
papers.abstract: Closely located urban and rural environments can differ in temperature, water availability, species diversity, and more. As a result, organisms in urban environments may experience different selection than those in rural environments. We investigated whether differences in selection might explain a previously identified urban-rural cline in the flower colour of Hesperis matronalis (dame's rocket). To explore whether plants in urban and rural environments are impacted by possible differences in pollinator availability or behavior, we performed a pollen supplementation experiment. We did not detect an effect of pollen supplementation on seed production in either setting (urban or rural), indicating that there is limited opportunity for any differences in pollinator availability or visitation to explain the cline in flower colour. We also measured the strength of selection acting on flower colour to investigate if it differed between urban and rural populations. In all but one population, we failed to detect significant linear or non-linear selection on flower colour, suggesting that selection on flower colour does not differ between urban and rural populations. Our results suggest that the urban-rural flower colour cline is likely not caused by differences in selection or pollen-limitation and may be due to stochastic forces.

papers.title: An elongated lifespan is associated with higher oxidative protection of flight tissue in Heliconiini butterflies
papers.abstract: Evolutionary theories of ageing often invoke trade-offs in resource allocation between somatic maintenance and other important physiological functions. One proposed mechanistic mediator of these trade-offs is oxidative stress, which arises from an imbalance between an organism's production of reactive oxygen species and its ability to detoxify them. Accordingly, many long-lived species across the animal kingdom show evidence for resistance to oxidative stress. However, it can be difficult to associate lifespan differences with oxidative phenotypes when comparing species across wide taxonomic distances, which may also show large differences in physiology. Butterflies in the long-lived Heliconius genus show a 3-fold lifespan extension and slowed ageing in comparison with their close relatives in the Heliconiini tribe, to whom they are phylogenetically, ecologically, and physiologically similar. However, proximate explanations for this extended longevity are currently lacking. Here, we leverage the neat comparative framework between Heliconius hecale and Dryas iulia, a shorter-lived Heliconiini outgroup, to test whether the observed lifespan differences between the two species are associated with differences in oxidative physiology. Our findings suggest superior oxidative protection of thoracic tissue in the longer-lived H. hecale compared to D. iulia, as evidenced by increased superoxide dismutase activity, increased total antioxidant capacity, and a corresponding reduction in lipid peroxidation in this tissue. Considering the metabolic demands of insect flight, we suggest that this oxidative phenotype may contribute to the extended longevity of Heliconius by enhancing protection of thoracic tissues against oxidative damage, representing a plausible proximate pro-longevity mechanism in this genus.

papers.title: High-content screening identifies FDA-approved activators of mitophagy
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial diseases are highly heterogeneous disorders caused by defects in oxidative phosphorylation, for which only limited therapeutic options are available. The elimination of dysfunctional mitochondria via mitophagy activation is an attractive strategy to treat several mitochondrial diseases, irrespective of the underlying genetic defect. To identify pharmacological activators of this pathway, we performed a high-content screening of 1,971 FDA-approved compounds using cellular reporters of TFEB nuclear translocation and mitophagy. This screening identified 294 compounds that promoted TFEB translocation, nine of which increased the number of mitolysosomes without compromising cell viability or damaging mitochondria. Among the selected compounds, Meptazinol and Ponatinib emerged as the top-ranked mitophagy inducers in fibroblasts from patients with complex I and IV deficiency, respectively, and were prioritised for further characterisation. However, they did not rescue the bioenergetic defect, suggesting that the stimulation of mitophagy per se is not sufficient to ameliorate the OXPHOS defect in mitochondrial diseases. Overall, our findings establish a scalable platform for the identification of pharmacological activators of TFEB and identify candidate compounds for therapeutic modulation of mitophagy.

papers.title: A LOV-domain photoreceptor mediates phototaxis in brown algae
papers.abstract: Phototaxis enables motile cells to navigate light environments and plays a critical role in survival and reproduction across diverse eukaryotic lineages. This ability has evolved independently through distinct photoreceptor systems. Yet, the molecular mechanisms underlying phototaxis remain poorly understood in many major eukaryotic lineages, including stramenopiles. Here, combining functional genetics, cell biology and evolutionary analyses, we identify Helmchrome (HELM), a LOV-domain protein required for phototaxis in the brown alga Ectocarpus. HELM localizes to the posterior flagellum and is responsible for the characteristic flavin-associated fluorescence of brown algal gametes. Loss of HELM abolishes phototactic accumulation and directional orientation without affecting basal motility or fertilization, demonstrating its specific requirement for light-directed movement. Phylogenetic analyses reveal that HELM-like proteins are distributed across diverse stramenopile lineages and that their domain architecture evolved through repeated duplication of an ancestral RGS-LOV module. Our findings identify HELM as a key component of the light-sensing machinery in brown algae, provide a molecular explanation for the long-standing observation of flagellar flavin fluorescence, and reveal a distinct phototaxis system that expands the known diversity of eukaryotic light-sensing mechanisms.

papers.title: A TMEM175 Mutation Disrupts the Lysosomal-Mitochondrial Axis Causing Short QT Syndrome and Sudden Cardiac Death
papers.abstract: Short QT Syndrome (SQTS) is a rare cardiac channelopathy characterized by abnormally short QTc intervals and increased sudden cardiac death (SCD) risk. Only 20-30% of SQTS cases have been linked to genetic mutations, typi-cally in surface membrane ion channels. We identified a novel lysosomal TMEM175 gene mutation (p.Arg377His) in 7 patients in a family with SQTS and SCD. Genetic analyses, including whole exome sequencing in the family and rare-variant burden testing in [~]118,000 UK Biobank participants, sug-gested an association between TMEM175 rare variants and QT interval short-ening. Functional studies in CRISPR-engineered mice and patient-specific induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (iPSC-CMs) revealed that TMEM175R377H causes shortened QT intervals and hastened repolariza-tion, respectively, as well an increased arrhythmia susceptibility. Isolated TMEM175R377H cardiomyocytes showed action potential duration (APD) abbre-viation, confirmed in whole TMEM175R377H mouse hearts and patient-specific iPSC-CM monolayers. In silico and electron microscopy studies showed that TMEM175R377H disrupts lysosomal-mitochondrial interactions, leading to mito-chondrial dysfunction, as evidenced by the reduced maximal respiration and spare respiratory capacity, with reduced ATP production, IKATP activation, and APD shortening. This mutation represents the first non-sarcolemmal ion chan-nel defect associated with SQTS and high SCD risk, potentially expanding the genetic landscape of the disease.

papers.title: LOca-1: A minimal calcium-activated arginyl-specific orthocaspase from the Loki's Castle hydrothermal vent field
papers.abstract: Orthocaspases are prokaryotic homologs of metacaspases within the C14 family of cysteine proteases, yet their biochemical properties and cellular roles remain poorly understood. Here, we report the discovery and comprehensive characterization of LOca-1, a metagenome-derived orthocaspase from the Loki's Castle hydrothermal vent field. LOca-1 consists primarily of a single, conserved p20 catalytic domain and undergoes calcium-dependent activation through cleavage at a conserved arginine residue. Once activated, LOca-1 displays strict arginyl-specific proteolytic activity and strong selectivity for residues surrounding the cleavage site. The enzyme is both thermoactive and thermostable, exhibiting maximal activity at 65 {degrees}C and a melting temperature of approximately 72 {degrees}C. Structural modelling revealed conservation of the catalytic core relative to plant metacaspases despite substantial sequence divergence. To our knowledge, LOca-1 is only the second biochemically characterized orthocaspase and the first reported from a deep-sea hydrothermal vent environment. LOca-1 expands the known biochemical diversity of prokaryotic metacaspase homologs and provides insights into the properties of a minimal p20-domain orthocaspase. Together, our findings establish LOca-1 as a thermostable, calcium-activated arginyl-specific orthocaspase and provide a foundation for future studies of orthocaspase function in prokaryotes.

papers.title: Nuclear retention and RNA editing safeguard self-tolerance to immunogenic intron lariats
papers.abstract: Introns are excised as lariats and rapidly degraded upon linearization, leaving their post-splicing role unclear. Here, we investigate their immunoregulatory potential by analyzing the intron lariat landscape upon inhibition of the debranching enzyme DBR1. We find that lariats harboring transposable elements (TEs), especially inverted Alu repeats (IRAlus), elicit cell cycle-dependent activation of protein kinase R (PKR), but only in cells harboring a high burden, such as breast cancer. These immunogenic lariats are initially retained in the nucleus, but upon cytosolic release, they drive PKR activation and apoptosis. Exploiting this, we combine DBR1 depletion with anti-mitotic chemotherapy to enhance lariat-PKR interactions and promote cancer cell death in vitro and in vivo. We further show that A-to-I editing of IRAlus-containing lariats weakens their interaction with PKR and suppresses PKR activation. Our findings highlight two parallel molecular mechanisms to sustain self-tolerance to repeat-rich introns, revealing a vulnerability exploitable for anti-tumor therapy.

papers.title: Viral replication and host response in airway epithelial cells predicts coronavirus pathogenicity and identifies HCoV-229E as an atypical seasonal coronavirus
papers.abstract: Human coronaviruses (HCoVs) range from mild seasonal strains to pathogenic viruses that cause severe pneumonia. The virological and host determinants that distinguish pathogenic coronaviruses (MERS-CoV, SARS-CoV-2) from seasonal strains (HCoV-229E, HCoV-NL63 and HCoV-OC43) remain poorly defined. To identify determinants of pathogenicity, we systematically compared replication, cellular tropism, innate responses and cytopathogenicity of pathogenic compared with seasonal HCoVs across nasal, bronchial, small airway and embryonic stem cell derived alveolar type II (AT2) epithelial cell cultures. All HCoVs preferentially infected ciliated cells in the upper airway, but only pathogenic viruses replicated to high titres in AT2 cells. Pathogenic HCoVs reprogrammed AT2 function and suppressed key innate immune signatures, consistent with distal lung epithelial dysfunction. In contrast, seasonal HCoVs were associated with limited alveolar replication and milder disruption of AT2 homeostasis. Strikingly, despite modest replication in all cell types, HCoV-229E induced pronounced epithelial injury, cilia loss and strong interferon stimulated gene expression, as well as induction of cellular stress/death programmes resembling those induced by MERS-CoV. These findings highlight the striking differences in cellular responses throughout the airways and between distinct HCoV strains and emphasizes the importance of assessing distal lung tropism and epithelial host responses to evaluate emergent coronaviruses to inform pandemic preparedness strategies.

papers.title: Characterization of Lactobacillus rhamnosus-Derived Extracellular Vesicles and Their Cellular Cytoprotective Effects Against Trimethylamine-Induced Oxidative Stress in Caco-2 Cells
papers.abstract: Dietary trimethylamine (TMA) underwent gut microbiota-mediated catabolism and subsequent hepatic oxidation to generate trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), a key metabolic factor linked to vascular and colorectal diseases. While the systemic effects of circulating TMAO were heavily investigated, the direct localized cellular interactions of its precursor, TMA, at the intestinal epithelial level required further elucidation. This study characterized extracellular vesicles isolated from Lactobacillus rhamnosus (Lr-EVs) and evaluated their cytoprotective potential in an in vitro human intestinal Caco-2 cell model under TMA-induced stress. Exposure to a high concentration of TMA (20 mM) significantly reduced Caco-2 viability to 78.8%, triggered intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation, and compromised tight junction integrity as observed via the disruption of Zonula Occludens-1 (ZO-1) alignment. Co-treatment with Lr-EVs (100-300 g/mL) counteracted this cellular toxicity, enhancing cell survival up to 172%. Quantitative PCR analysis revealed that Lr-EVs suppressed the transcriptional upregulation of the pro-inflammatory gene IL-1{beta}, restored the expression of the metabolic regulator SIRT1, and stabilized transcript levels of key mitochondrial-encoded electron transport chain genes (ND6, CYTB, CO1, and ATP6). Additionally, Lr-EVs exhibited intrinsic radical scavenging activities in cell-free ABTS and DPPH assays. These preliminary in vitro findings demonstrated that Lr-EVs mitigated TMA-induced cellular injury, oxidative stress, and junctional disruption at the transcriptomic level, supporting further investigation of probiotic-derived EVs as prospective cell-free functional ingredients.

papers.title: Novel viral diversity and geographic structuring in the New Zealand West Coast blackfly (Austrosimulium ungulatum)
papers.abstract: Background Vector-borne diseases represent a major global public health burden, with climate change, land-use change and increasing human activity altering arthropod vector distributions and creating opportunities for infectious disease emergence. In Aotearoa New Zealand, insects commonly referred to as "sandflies" are blackflies belonging to the family Simuliidae. The West Coast blackfly, Austrosimulium ungulatum, is an endemic, human-biting species abundant throughout the South Island, yet its associated viral diversity remains largely unexplored. Methods Here, we used metatranscriptomic sequencing to characterise the virome of the West Coast blackfly and investigate patterns of viral diversity and community composition across geographical and environmental gradients. A total of 425 blackflies were collected from 19 locations spanning approximately 187 km. Results We identified 94 viral sequences across 16 orders and six phyla, all of which were putatively novel viruses. These included divergent lineages within families containing recognised vertebrate and arthropod pathogens, such as the Rhabdoviridae and Orthomyxoviridae. Viral community composition varied among sampling locations, but no significant associations were detected between land-use categories and viral diversity or community composition. In contrast, we revealed a weak but significant positive correlation between geographical distance and viral community dissimilarity, suggesting some degree of spatial structuring across the sampling range. Conclusions This study provides the first metatranscriptomic characterisation of the virome associated with the endemic West Coast blackfly, revealing substantial previously undescribed viral diversity and providing insights into the geographical distribution of arthropod-associated viral communities.

papers.title: Structural basis of virion assembly in the Mycobacterium tuberculosis-infecting mycobacteriophage SWU1
papers.abstract: The rising threat of drug-resistant tuberculosis has renewed interest in bacteriophage therapy as an urgently needed alternative. Rational engineering of these viruses, however, requires an atomic-level understanding of virion architecture. Mycobacteriophage SWU1 belongs to subcluster A2, one of the few mycobacteriophage lineages known to infect Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M. tuberculosis). Using single-particle cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM), we resolved essentially the entire SWU1 virion architecture by localized reconstruction of four modules, the capsid, portal vertex, tail and baseplate, at resolutions of 3.62 [A], 3.51 [A], 3.70 [A] and 3.22 [A], respectively. The T=7 capsid comprises 415 copies of an HK97-fold major capsid protein and lacks any decoration protein in density. The 12-fold portal reconciles its C5-C12 mismatch with the capsid vertex through defined, non-equivalent subunit contacts. The baseplate carries a 13-fold tail-fiber ring on a 6-fold hub, a geometry without precedent among characterized phages, established here by symmetry-free reconstruction. These findings provide the critical insights into the assembly and infection of SWU1, laying a structural foundation for the future optimization of phage-based anti-TB therapeutics.

papers.title: Metagenomic Insights into the Fecal Microbiome, Resistome, and Mobilome of Beef Cattle in Cow-Calf Operations in Florida, United States
papers.abstract: Food-producing animals are a focus of One Health approaches to antimicrobial resistance (AMR) as reservoirs of antimicrobial-resistant bacteria (ARB) and antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs). We hypothesized that microbial composition, ARGs profiles, and mobile genetic element (MGE) profiles would differ by operation size and animal age group. Fecal samples from 162 cows and calves were combined into 54 composite samples, each comprising three animals of the same age group. Across operation sizes, Bacillota (51.4-64.9%), Bacteroidota (12.0-17.3%), Pseudomonadota (10.3-16.5%), and Actinomycetota (3.3-10.9%) were predominant phyla. Alpha diversity did not differ among operation sizes; however, cows exhibited greater observed richness, Shannon diversity, and Simpson diversity than calves (all P < 0.001). Microbial composition did not differ significantly among operation sizes (PERMANOVA, R{superscript 2} = 0.065, P = 0.609) but differed significantly between cows and calves (R{superscript 2} = 0.200, P < 0.001). Seventy-five ARGs representing 14 resistance classes were identified. Normalized ARG hit rates were higher in small operations (0.444) than in medium (0.278) and large operations (0.222; P = 0.088), whereas calves exhibited a higher estimated marginal mean normalized ARG hit rate than cows (0.383 vs. 0.247 hits/million reads; P < 0.001). Of 1,054 curated ARG hits, 23.9% occurred on predicted plasmid contigs, 0.9% on predicted viral contigs, and 7.1% on contigs containing insertion sequences. Overall findings demonstrate differences in fecal microbiome diversity and ARG abundance between cows and calves and indicate that predicted plasmids are associated with a notable proportion of ARG hits in Florida beef cow-calf operations.

papers.title: Large seed size accompanying GmSDP1 suppression is linked to cellular remodeling and phytohormone regulation
papers.abstract: Soybean (Glycine max) seeds contain approximately 20% oil and 40% protein and are important for food, feed, and biofuel. Improving soybean productivity and seed quality requires optimizing carbon partitioning during seed development. Previously, seed-specific suppression of the lipase-encoding gene Sugar-Dependent 1 (SDP1) increased seed oil content by approximately 5% while slightly reducing raffinose family oligosaccharides without compromising protein content. Seed-specific SDP1 suppression also increased seed size by 18-25% without affecting seed number, resulting in greater seed biomass per plant. To determine the developmental basis of the increased seed size, we investigated the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying this phenotype. Microscopy and biochemical analyses showed that larger seeds were associated with increased seed cell size and enhanced lignocellulosic cell wall accumulation. Temporal biochemical and transcriptomic analyses further revealed coordinated changes in hormone homeostasis, including altered levels of abscisic acid, 12-oxo-phytodienoic acid, and jasmonoyl-isoleucine, together with differential expression of F-box and RING/U-box family genes. The results indicate that the enhanced seed size resulting from SDP1 suppression is associated with coordinated changes in cellular development, cell wall accumulation, hormone homeostasis, and regulation of gene expression during seed development. Developmental and metabolic changes associated with the increased seed size phenotype support SDP1 manipulation as a potential strategy for improving soybean seed yield and quality.

papers.title: Choline kinase A is required for alkylating agent resistance via lipid droplet formation
papers.abstract: Tolerance of DNA damage promotes cellular fitness, particularly in cancer cells under chemotherapeutic pressure. However, the biology and regulation of DNA damage responses remain incompletely understood. Using an unbiased genetic screen, we found that choline kinase A (CHKA) is required for alkylating resistance in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL). CHKA is best-known as a cytoplasmic enzyme that catalyzes the first step in phosphatidylcholine biosynthesis, but alkylating agent resistance was mediated by a nuclear function of CHKA. We found that CHKA positively regulates transcription of the DNA repair factor RAD51 via formation of lipid droplets. Restoring lipid droplet formation or RAD51 expression was sufficient to confer alkylating agent resistance despite CHKA inactivation. Our findings link lipid droplet formation to transcriptional control of the DNA damage response, providing a mechanism through which cellular lipid metabolism can control the maintenance of genome integrity.

papers.title: DIALECT: DNA-Programmable Synthetic Cells Communicate with Mammalian Cells through Synthetic Receptors
papers.abstract: Synthetic cells can regulate mammalian signalling through the controlled release of diffusible protein ligands, but coupling programmable synthetic-cell senders to orthogonal, engineered mammalian receptors remains challenging. Here we present DIALECT (DNA-Instructed Assembly of Ligands for Engineered Cellular Transduction), a platform in which proteinosome-based synthetic cells translate sequence-defined DNA inputs into coiled-coil signalling ligand outputs for engineered mammalian receptors. DNA-ligand conjugates are localized within semipermeable proteinosomes through DNA hybridization and released by toehold-mediated DNA strand displacement (TMSD). The released ligands diffuse to neighbouring mammalian cells and activate cognate CC-GEMS receptors, inducing JAK/STAT3 signalling and reporter activation, with a higher response in cognate than non-cognate receiver cells under activation conditions. We further implement distributed Boolean AND logic using two independently programmed proteinosome populations that respond to distinct DNA inputs and release complementary ligand components. Simultaneous addition of both inputs produces substantially higher reporter activity than the respective single-input conditions, consistent with extracellular assembly of an active receptor agonist. DIALECT thus establishes a modular interface linking DNA-based molecular computation in synthetic cells to orthogonal signalling pathways in mammalian cells, providing a foundation for hybrid artificial-biological communication networks.

papers.title: ERV-derived dsRNAs induce stress granules that drive neural crest fate to initiate melanoma
papers.abstract: Melanoma arises when melanocytes are oncogenically reprogrammed into neural crest-like cells, but what initiates this switch is unknown. Here we show that endogenous retrovirus (ERV)-derived double stranded RNAs (dsRNAs) induce stress granules (SGs) that drive this fate change. In zebrafish, melanoma progresses through a stage-specific ERV switch: zferv marks precursor cells before crestin activates in tumor cells. Both elements generate dsRNA that triggers eif2ak2-dependent SGs within precursor lesions and through transformation. SGs are tumorigenic as G3BP1 overexpression accelerates melanoma onset, whereas mosaic, melanocyte-specific g3bp1/2 knockout delays it. Small molecule-mediated inhibition of G3BP1/2 eliminates precursor lesions and reduces tumor burden. Similarly, blocking dsRNA sensing prevents SG formation and lowers melanoma incidence. Human nevi and melanomas show analogous, stage-specific ERV programs and SG assembly. In human melanoma cells, SGs sequester and translationally repress SOX10-regulating mRNAs, including the tumor suppressor KMT2D. Mosaic knockout of kmt2d in vivo enhances SOX10-driven neural crest reactivation. Thus, an ERV-SG axis establishes an oncogenic translatome that enables melanoma fate, with diagnostic and therapeutic potential.

papers.title: Dietary fibre combinations modulate gut microbiome composition and metabolic responses in zebrafish, with lasting effects on intestinal barrier gene expression
papers.abstract: Food sources provide a complex mixture of dietary fibres, not a single type. Consuming a diverse range of these dietary fibre-containing foods is associated with health benefits. However, how the effects of combining dietary fibres translate across different biological levels remains poorly characterised. This study uses an integrated microbiome-metabolome analytical approach that combines 16S rRNA gene sequencing with metabolomic profiling of the intestine, brain and liver. Specifically, we examined the combined effects of apple pectin (AP) and cellulose (C) within the same diet, compared with their isolated effects, in adult female and male zebrafish (Danio rerio). Notably, the combined apple pectin and cellulose diet (APC) produced a microbiome composition that could not be predicted by simply adding the changes observed with each dietary fibre individually, indicating a significant non-additive interaction between the two dietary components, specifically a less-than-additive response in gut microbiome composition. The resulting community composition under the combined diet also more closely resembled that induced by apple pectin. We found that predicted microbial functional capabilities did not translate directly into quantified intestinal and brain short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) concentrations, nor did intestinal SCFA levels directly mirror those observed in the brain. Moreover, we used targeted qPCR gene expression analysis to assess responses to a subsequent saponin challenge after dietary fibre cessation, revealing a potentially protective effect on the intestinal barrier. Collectively, we show that dietary fibres within the same diet interact to shape the gut microbiome and do not act in isolation, leading to non-linear health ramifications for the host that may persist even after active consumption ends.

papers.title: BCAS3 regulates WIPI2b via a direct interaction in the ATG16L1-binding cleft
papers.abstract: De novo formation of the phagophore membrane is a fundamental step in autophagy and relies on recruitment of the E3-like ligase complex via an interaction between ATG16L1 and phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PtdIns3P)-effector protein, WIPI2b. Although WIPI2b can directly bind membranes, how its membrane association is regulated is still not fully understood. Here, we describe BCAS3 as a novel direct interactor of WIPI2b and demonstrate that a peptide of BCAS3 binds in the ATG16L1-binding cleft of WIPI2b with low micromolar affinity. We show that BCAS3 and its partner PHAF1 induce recruitment of WIPI2b to membranes via the interaction of BCAS3 with PtdIns3P. This not only challenges the current paradigm, whereby ATG16L1 is the only confirmed binder of WIPI2b in this region, but also offers a mechanism through which WIPI2b membrane association might be regulated.

papers.title: Stathmin-2 regulates microtubule dynamics and axonal resilience in human motor neurons
papers.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is characterized by the selective degeneration of motor neurons, yet the mechanisms that either induce neurodegeneration or confer neuronal resilience remain poorly understood. Loss of the microtubule-associated protein Stathmin-2 (STMN2) is a downstream consequence of TDP-43 pathology present in nearly all cases of ALS and has emerged as a central feature of disease. However, the mechanisms by which STMN2 maintains homeostasis in motor neurons remain incompletely defined. Here, we investigated the role of STMN2 in regulating cytoskeletal organization and axonal function. Using TIRF microscopy, we quantified STMN2-dependent changes in microtubule growth and catastrophe at single-microtubule resolution. In human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived motor neurons, STMN2 depletion increased baseline rates of microtubule polymerization. However, STMN2 depletion impaired recovery of axonal microtubules following transient nocodazole-induced depolymerization, indicating that STMN2 is required for efficient cytoskeletal remodeling after stress. Consistent with these findings, STMN2-depleted neurons exhibited impaired microtubule recovery following acute depolymerization and reduced axonal recoil after optically induced local microtubule severing. Finally, STMN2 depletion disrupted the formation of neuromuscular junction-like contacts in human motor neuron-myocyte co-cultures, linking impaired cytoskeletal homeostasis to loss of distal neuronal connectivity. Together, these findings identify STMN2 as a key regulator of cytoskeletal resilience that coordinates microtubule remodeling, mitochondrial transport, and maintenance of neuromuscular junctions. We propose that impaired resilience of the axonal cytoskeleton represents a critical point of vulnerability in motor neurons in patients with ALS, establishing cytoskeletal resilience as a potential therapeutic target downstream of TDP-43 pathology.

papers.title: Dynamic regulation of single-cell contractile heterogeneity in the human trabecular meshwork
papers.abstract: Altered trabecular meshwork (TM) mechanics contribute to increased aqueous humor outflow resistance and elevated intraocular pressure in glaucoma, yet how contractility is regulated across individual TM cells remains poorly understood. Using a high-throughput single-cell contractility assay, we quantified time-resolved contractile behavior in primary human TM cells under defined extracellular matrix (ECM) compositions, substrate stiffnesses, and pharmacologic perturbations, and related functional mechanical behavior to intracellular protein abundance. Single-cell analyses revealed that TM contractility is not a uniform population property but a context-dependent contractile state shaped by both extracellular and intracellular regulation. ECM composition established distinct contractile programs, with collagen IV promoting rapid convergence toward a highly contractile state, collagen I supporting a slower but similar response, and fibronectin maintaining a persistently heterogeneous low-contractility state. In contrast, the intracellular perturbation dexamethasone (DEX) did not uniformly increase contractility but selectively prolonged contractile activity within the most mechanically active cells, thereby sustaining highly contractile states. This response was progressively constrained as ECM stiffness increased and was absent on pathologically stiff substrates, demonstrating that extracellular mechanical context conditions glucocorticoid responsiveness. Conversely, ROCK inhibition overrode both basal and DEX-induced contractile programs, collapsing the heterogeneous population into a uniformly low-contractility state. Finally, intracellular protein abundance poorly predicted functional mechanical behavior, with weak pooled associations reflecting divergent donor-specific relationships rather than consistent molecular-mechanical coupling. Together, these findings show that TM contractility emerges from integrating intrinsic cellular state and the extracellular mechanical environment rather than from either alone. More broadly, they identify single-cell contractile state as a functional dimension of TM cell identity that cannot be inferred from static molecular marker abundance or population-averaged mechanical measurements.

papers.title: Rapid generation of marsupial induced pluripotent stem cells suitable for use in next-generation conservation
papers.abstract: Marsupials account for a disproportionate share of recent and impending mammalian extinctions, that has prompted investment in the development of "next generation" conservation biotechnologies. These include the generation of genetically selected/modified individuals for improved population fitness. Given the inherent limitations of working with threatened species, a flexible vehicle to develop these technologies is through the generation and editing of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). However, it is deemed necessary to derive transgene-free iPSCs for conservation target species, which can be highly time consuming and expensive. This study describes the generation of iPSCs from the marsupial fat-tailed dunnart (diPSCs) that serves as a model species for next generation conservation initiatives. These diPSCs exhibit features of totipotency when cells are maintained with exogenous reprogramming factors for long periods, until differentiation potential is required. Neonatal dunnart fibroblasts were reprogrammed using doxycycline-inducible Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, Lin28 and Myc, and the resulting iPSC lines were characterised at the transcriptomic, epigenetic and functional level (trilineage differentiation, embryoid body formation and mouse blastocyst injection assays). Dunnart iPSCs exhibited robust transcriptional and epigenetic activation of core pluripotency factors (POU5F1, POU5F3, SALL4) as well as factors associated with the naive and primed states of eutherian pluripotency (TBX3, KLF2, TFCP2L1, SOX11, DNMT3A). Dunnart iPSCs readily differentiated in trilineage and embryoid body formation assays, where they expressed markers of all three germ lineages. When injected into 8-cell mouse blastocysts, dunnart iPSCs integrated into both the inner cell mass and trophoblast, reflecting a capacity to contribute to embryonic and extra embryonic lineages during early development. Further, we show that diPSCs can maintain their potential in the presence of exogenous pluripotency factors, until required for differentiation. This robust iPSC generation and maintenance approach is a valuable avenue for the rapid application of next-generation conservation technologies in threatened species.

papers.title: SeekNSee: A Rule-Based Framework for Prioritizing Proteotypic Peptides
papers.abstract: Selecting peptides candidates for target proteomics requires integrating a multicriteria problem, particularly when users lack prior experimental data, programming expertise, or stable access to external repositories. We development SeekNSee, a locally executed R/Shiny application designed to improve the reproducibility and auditability of peptide-candidate screening through enzyme-aware in silico digestion, configurable and traceable rule-level decision tracking. Starting from a user provided reference proteome and target sequences, SeekNSee generates peptides-candidates using nine digestion configurations and evaluates them with 12 rules configured as ignore, apply, or block. Numerical score and retained/blocking status are stored independently, and every candidate-rule outcome is preserved in a rule-level trace. Computational validation confirmed the specified behavior in controlled cases through 198 passing automated assertions, complemented by successful operational and processing tests on Windows and Ubuntu. Proteome-wide application covered all 20,416 reviewed human proteins, generating 733,864 peptide-candidate and 581,026 unique peptides sequences while preserving data integrity, decision traceability, and candidate-specific context. DIA, DDA, and deep-fractionated proteomics benchmarking showed strong associations between SeekNSee scores categories, peptide observation, and multiple analytical measurements. Together, these results support that SeekNSee provides a transparent and traceable screening layer for generating peptide-candidates for subsequent assay and experimental validation.

papers.title: Mucin promotes pneumococcal colonization via autolysis suppression and tryptophan-mediated immune modulation
papers.abstract: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a leading human respiratory pathogen, yet its success depends not on disease but on its ability to persist as an asymptomatic colonizer of the nasopharynx. The nasopharyngeal mucosa is lined with mucus, whose heavily O-glycosylated mucin proteins are the most abundant macromolecules in the pneumococcal natural niche. While mucus is canonically viewed as a host defense barrier, we found that mucin actively reprograms pneumococcal physiology to promote colonization through two distinct mechanisms. First, mucin suppresses pneumococcal autolysis by specifically inhibiting the enzymatic activity of the major autolysin LytA, prolonging bacterial survival and restricting release of the cholesterol-dependent cytotoxin pneumolysin, thereby reducing host cell damage. Second, mucin induces de novo biosynthesis and extracellular release of tryptophan, an essential amino acid that humans cannot synthesize and that serves as a substrate for host immunomodulatory pathways. Tryptophan biosynthesis was critical for pneumococcal survival against macrophage killing, and its disruption abolished both colonization and invasive disease. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that tryptophan biosynthesis enables the pneumococcus to survive a bactericidal macrophage state while preventing macrophage transition to proliferative tissue repair. Together, these findings reveal that mucin is not merely a barrier but an active signal that reprograms the pneumococcus toward a persistent, host-tolerant state, identifying a distinctive repertoire of colonization mechanisms that allow a virulent respiratory pathogen to sustain long-term asymptomatic carriage in its human reservoir.

papers.title: Intracellular bio-synthesizing Gold Nanoparticles using bacterial systems and their applications in photothermal therapy (A green approach)
papers.abstract: Background: Conventional cancer therapies are heavily constrained by systemic toxicity, off-target side effects, and poor deep-tissue penetration due to the highly heterogeneous tumor microenvironment (TME). Although gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) possess exceptional localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) properties ideal for photothermal therapy (PTT), their clinical translation is bottlenecked by inconsistent passive accumulation and chemical toxicity arising from conventional synthetic surfactants. Objective: This study developed a sustainable, biocompatible bio-hybrid platform utilizing the probiotic Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 (EcN) as an autonomous, tumor-homing living carrier integrated with AuNPs synthesized via an eco-friendly intracellular green chemistry approach. Methods: EcN cultures were prepared in Luria-Bertani (LB) medium and subsequently exposed to a 1 mM chloroauric acid (HAuCl4) metallic precursor. A facile, room-temperature green synthesis protocol was established by utilizing ascorbic acid (Vitamin C) as a non-toxic co-reductant to drive a seed-mediated crystallization onto intra-bacterial metallic seeds. The bio-hybrid system (EcN::AuNPs) was characterized via visual inspection, UV-Vis spectroscopy, and in vitro PTT assays under continuous-wave near-infrared (NIR) laser irradiation. Results: Visual confirmation showed an irreversible color shift from pale yellow to a deep dark-brownish hue, serving as a direct diagnostic indicator of successful Au3+ to Au0 reduction. UV-Vis spectroscopic analysis revealed a distinct, broadened surface plasmon resonance (SPR) band centered at 560nm, indicating the formation of stabilized, isotropic gold nanostructures (30-60nm) subjected to near-field electromagnetic coupling within the complex intracellular compartments (periplasm and cytoplasm). Biocompatibility assays demonstrated a significant collapse in cell viability from 10^8CFU/mL down to 10^3CFU/mL, driven by a combination of trivalent gold heavy-metal toxicity, mechanical disruption of the peptidoglycan wall from spatial confinement, and severe metabolic/oxidative stress. Nevertheless, the remaining surviving population maintained required active chemotactic capabilities, while the lysed bacterial matrix provided a natural protein capping layer that prevented nanoparticle aggregation. Under 5 minutes of continuous NIR laser irradiation, the EcN::AuNPs platform exhibited exceptional concentration-dependent hyperthermia kinetics, triggering a drastic thermal escalation from 20 C to an absolute peak of 75.4 C, vastly outperforming all baseline control groups (pure EcN, bare HAuCl4, and standalone ascorbic acid). Conclusion: The engineered EcN::AuNPs bio-hybrid platform represents a highly efficient and biosafe "bacteriobot" paradigm. By shifting the SPR footprint and leveraging the native bacterial cell envelope for colloidal stability, this system achieves an optimal equilibrium between active biological tumor targeting and rapid, localized photothermal ablation, offering a promising alternative for targeted oncological interventions.

papers.title: Targeted Deletions Uncover Previously Uncharacterised C1-fixing Cluster Genes as Essential for Autotrophy in Clostridium autoethanogenum
papers.abstract: Recycling carbon oxides from industrial off-gases and gasified organic waste using gas fermentation offers a sustainable route for biomanufacturing of fuels and chemicals. Acetogens are attractive biocatalysts here and fix CO and CO2 via the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway (WLP). However, the incomplete functional annotation of the associated C1-fixing gene cluster limits rational engineering of acetogen cell factories. Here, we investigated five highly conserved but previously uncharacterised C1-fixing cluster genes to quantify their contributions to the growth of the model-acetogen Clostridium autoethanogenum using targeted CRISPR/Cas9-mediated single-gene deletions, physiological characterisation, comparative computational structural analyses, CRISPRi, and functional genomics. Importantly, we identified acsV, lpdA, cooC, and cooC2 as essential for autotrophy but not heterotrophy, whereas deletion of gcvH reduced autotrophic growth and shifted carbon flux from acetate towards 2,3-butanediol. Amino acid supplementation experiments and computational analyses indicate that lpdA and gcvH do not primarily function in glycine or serine biosynthesis but instead fulfil specialised roles in WLP-associated C1 and redox metabolism. Furthermore, genetic and physiological analyses showed that the two CooC-family ATPases, CooC and CooC2, have non-redundant roles in growth, with only cooC2 deletion impairing heterotrophy. Acetate supplementation tests revealed that {Delta}acsV cells retained metabolic activity despite abolished autotrophy, and computational analyses suggest a likely role for acsV in ATP-dependent corrinoid activation. Surprisingly, CRISPRi-mediated repression of acsV was translationally buffered, resulting in altered carbon partitioning without impairing autotrophy. Together, our findings provide insights into the physiological importance of the C1-fixing cluster genes in acetogens and support their metabolic engineering as gas-fermenting cell factories.
